This document explains the choices behind RADdiversity: recommendations
for how the data should be filtered, which estimators are used and why,
which Stacks file to use for which statistic, how uncertainty is
measured, and why a test between populations must count both the
individuals and the loci. It is written for readers who know what
heterozygosity is but have not had to choose between estimators before.

To see the analysis itself step by step, start with
`vignette("workflow", package = "RADdiversity")`.

> **Where the numbers come from.** Simulation results quoted here can be
> re-run: Appendix C lists each one with the script or function that
> produces it (`inst/sims/` in the installed package, or a self-test
> function). Where a statement rests on the Stacks source code, the file
> and version are named.
>
> **Command line.** Every analysis can also be run from a shell with the
> scripts in `system.file("scripts", package = "RADdiversity")`, e.g.
> `Rscript diversity_stats.R populations.haps.vcf popmap.tsv --g=20`.
> The R functions are used throughout this document.

## 1. Getting the data

### Genotypes backed by few reads

A genotype is called from the reads that happened to be sequenced. If a
true heterozygote is covered by only a few reads, all of them may come
from the same chromosome, and it is called homozygous. With *d* reads
the chance of that is 2<sup>1−*d*</sup>:

| reads backing the genotype | chance a heterozygote shows only one allele |
|----------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| 3                          | 25%                                         |
| 5                          | 6%                                          |
| 10                         | 0.2%                                        |

Stacks' `populations --min-gt-depth 6` (Stacks 2.67 and later) sets such
genotypes to missing, as does `filter_genotype_depth(H, min_dp = 6)` in
R. The missing-data rate rises, but a visible gap is better than a
hidden error. Both treat heterozygous and homozygous calls alike, which
matters: a filter that removed heterozygotes more readily than
homozygotes (as `filter_low_conf_alt()` does) would itself bias Ho down
and FIS up.

Note that the table is about the reads, not about the genotype caller.
Stacks' `gstacks` calls a genotype only when the best genotype beats the
next one in a likelihood-ratio test (`--gt-alpha`, default 0.05), and
otherwise leaves it missing (`models.cc`, Stacks 2.68). Its default
model also weighs the population's genotype frequencies. So at the
lowest depths, many heterozygotes that show one allele become missing
rather than false homozygotes, and the table overstates the error
there. How many depends on the allele frequencies.

### Missing data: filter within populations

Stacks offers two missing-data filters that look alike:

- `-r 0.8 -p 2`: keep a locus if at least 80% of individuals **within
  each population** are genotyped, in at least 2 populations;
- `-R 0.8`: keep a locus if at least 80% of **all individuals pooled**
  are genotyped.

With the pooled rule (i.e., `-R`), a locus can pass by being well
genotyped in a large population while mostly missing in a small one. The
small population then carries more missing data than the large one, and
any effect of missing data on heterozygosity or FIS differs between
exactly the two samples being compared. Therefore, this package
recommends using `-r` with `-p` equal to the number of populations, or
`filter_call_rate(H, min_call, popmap = pops)` in R.

### Allele-frequency filters

Minor allele count and frequency filters (`--min-mac`, `--min-maf`) are
standard for RAD-seq data, and useful for analyses that are sensitive to
genotyping errors in rare variants (STRUCTURE, PCA, kinship). For
diversity statistics it helps to know what they remove. Rare variants
are real diversity: under a neutral site frequency spectrum, a site
whose derived allele is carried by *i* of *N* gene copies contributes to
π in proportion to *N* − *i*, so sites with a minor allele count of 2 or
less hold about 4/(*N* − 1) of π:

| diploids in the run | share of π at sites with minor allele count ≤ 2 |
|---------------------|-------------------------------------------------|
| 10                  | 21%                                             |
| 20                  | 10%                                             |
| 30                  | 7%                                              |

The share depends on sample size, so a MAC filter lowers per-site
diversity more in a small study than in a large one. The same spectrum
says what share of the SNPs such a filter removes: a site with *i*
derived copies is found in proportion to 1/*i*, so sites with a minor
allele count of 2 or less are (1 + 1/2 + 1/(*N* − 2) + 1/(*N* − 1)) /
(1 + 1/2 + … + 1/(*N* − 1)) of the SNPs, 36.5% at 20 diploids. The
filter removes many SNPs but little diversity. Stacks does not
delete a SNP that fails the filter: it turns it into a fixed site
(`LocusFilter::erase_snp()`, Stacks 2.68), so the site still counts in
`Sites` and the loss shows up in Stacks' own all-positions `Pi` as well.
Allelic richness and rarefied private alleles lose even more, because
rare alleles are what they count. None of this makes filtered data
unusable; it makes the threshold part of what a reported value means, so
state it, and compare values only between datasets filtered the same
way. If you control the pipeline, a separate unfiltered run for
diversity statistics avoids the question.

### Hardy-Weinberg filters

A Hardy-Weinberg filter removes loci with a heterozygote deficit, which
is what inbreeding produces, so it removes the signal FIS measures.
Filtering on HWE with all populations pooled is worse: differences in
allele frequency between populations look like heterozygote deficits
(the Wahlund effect), so the loci most informative about population
structure are removed (Pearman et al. 2022). RADdiversity's `hwe_test()`
reports departures but nothing in the package removes loci on them
(section 7). Some population genetics analyses may warrant removing loci
outside HWE (e.g., effective population size with certain methods), but
filtering should be done in another program like *populations*.

`--max-obs-het` is different: it removes sites where most individuals
are heterozygous, a crude screen for paralogs (two similar genomic
regions assembled as one locus), and is reasonable to use.

### Data filtered before they reach the package

Many VCFs arrive already filtered. The analyses still run; the table in
`vignette("workflow")` ("If your data were already filtered") lists what
each common filter changes and what to report, and `summary()` of a
`diversity_stats()` result shows what the data look filtered at when you ask
for `summary(details = TRUE)` (the rarest allele count left, the lowest call
rates, the highest per-record Ho); the short `summary()` says whether the data
look filtered by minor allele count. An HWE filter cannot be detected from the
data.

### Which records each population uses

`diversity_stats()` uses a record for a population once that population
has at least `min_n` genotyped individuals there (default 2, the
smallest number for which He and FIS are defined). This is decided for
each population separately, so an individual missing in one population
does not cost the other population that record. Every record counts
equally in FIS, however many individuals are typed there. No correction
for this is needed, because Ho and He at each record are unbiased on
their own, so their sums are too. Records with few typed individuals
only add noise. `diversity_core_selftest()` checks by simulation that
FIS stays unbiased when missingness is clustered by locus, as it is in
real RAD data. (That check makes genotypes go missing at random.
Missingness that depends on the genotype, such as allele dropout, is
covered in section 5.)

One consequence: two populations can rest on somewhat different records.
With `-p` equal to the number of populations (above) the sets are nearly
the same. Compare `Ar_n` between populations; the printed result and the
`CHECKS` of `summary()` add a note when one population's Ar rests on under 90%
as many records as another population's.

`complete_case = TRUE` uses a record only if every individual of every
population is genotyped there (Schmidt et al. 2021, recommendation (b)).
Records survive that rule at a rate of about (1 − *m*)<sup>*n*</sup> for
a missing-genotype rate *m* spread over *n* individuals, which falls
quickly:

| missing rate *m* | records surviving with 25 individuals |
|------------------|---------------------------------------|
| 2%               | 60%                                   |
| 5%               | 28%                                   |
| 10%              | 7%                                    |

A small, possibly unrepresentative subset of loci is a bigger problem
than missing data handled locus by locus, so the default is the
per-population rule; use `complete_case = TRUE` as a sensitivity
analysis.

## 2. The estimators

### One parameter, several names

Expected heterozygosity (He), gene diversity (Hs) and nucleotide
diversity (π) are all estimates of **one parameter**: the probability
that two gene copies drawn at random from a population differ. They
differ in two ways.

- **What is averaged over.** He is usually averaged over the variant
  records a study called. π is the same quantity averaged over **every
  sequenced site**, monomorphic ones included. Because most sites are
  monomorphic, π is orders of magnitude smaller than He from the same
  data, and He per variant site depends on how many variants a study
  happened to call, while π does not.
- **Which estimator.** The plug-in 1 − Σ*p*<sup>2</sup> is biased low in
  small samples; the two usual corrections are discussed next.

There is one more distinction at haplotype loci. At a biallelic site,
gene diversity and π per site are the same thing. At a multi-allelic RAD
haplotype locus, gene diversity treats any two different haplotypes as
simply "different", while nucleotide diversity would count how many
bases differ. So on a haplotype VCF nothing is nucleotide diversity,
whatever it is called.

In RADdiversity's output, `He` is always per variant record,
`He_autosomal` (from `diversity_stats(sites = )`) and `pi_nc` (from
`pi_allsites()`) are per sequenced site.

### Why Nei & Chesser's He

For a sample of *N* diploid individuals with allele frequencies
*p*<sub>i</sub> and observed heterozygosity *H*<sub>o</sub>, three
estimators are in use:

| estimator | formula | expectation, for true diversity *H* and inbreeding *F* |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| plug-in (Stacks `Exp_Het`) | 1 − Σ*p*<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup> | *H* (2*N* − 1 − *F*)/(2*N*) |
| 2*N*-corrected (Stacks `Pi`) | (2*N*/(2*N* − 1))(1 − Σ*p*<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup>) | *H* (1 − *F*/(2*N* − 1)) |
| Nei & Chesser (1983) | (*N*/(*N* − 1))(1 − Σ*p*<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup> − *H*<sub>o</sub>/(2*N*)) | *H* |

The 2*N*-corrected estimator treats the 2*N* gene copies as independent
draws, which is true only when *F* = 0. When individuals are inbred, it
runs low by the factor *F*/(2*N* − 1), usually well under 1%. Nei &
Chesser's estimator uses *H*<sub>o</sub> to remove that dependence and
is unbiased at any *F*; it is also what hierfstat reports as Hs.

The small bias matters for FIS, which divides by He. With the
2*N*-corrected He, FIS is pulled toward zero by roughly a factor 1/(2*N*
− 1): about 3% at *N* = 15 and 5% at *N* = 10. Because this depends on
*N*, it does not cancel when two populations of different size are
compared. It also sets the wrong limit: when every individual is
heterozygous at a biallelic locus, the true FIS is −1, but 1 −
*H*<sub>o</sub>/`Pi` gives −(*N* − 1)/*N* (−0.9 at *N* = 10); the Nei &
Chesser version gives −1. `diversity_core_selftest()` checks all of this
by simulation.

`diversity_stats()` reports both estimators side by side in
`estimator_comparison` (`He_NeiChesser`, `He_2n_corr`), so values from
other software can be reconciled.

### Why F<sub>IS</sub> is a ratio of sums

F<sub>IS</sub> combines thousands of loci. It can be computed per locus
and then averaged ("mean of ratios"), or computed once from the sums
over loci: F<sub>IS</sub> = 1 − ΣH<sub>o</sub>/ΣH<sub>s</sub> ("ratio of
sums"). A batting average is the everyday version: adding every hit and
every at-bat gives the team's average; averaging each player's own
average counts the pitcher who batted twice as much as the regular who
batted 600 times.

Loci differ enormously in how much they say about FIS: a nearly
monomorphic locus has He near zero and a per-locus FIS that is almost
pure noise. The ratio of sums weights each locus by its He, which is the
weighting used by Weir & Cockerham (1984) and recommended for combining
loci (Bhatia et al. 2013 make the same point for F<sub>ST</sub>). A
locus monomorphic in a population contributes 0 to both sums, so whether
such loci are included does not change the result.

Stacks reports F<sub>IS</sub> as a mean of per-site ratios, counting
sites monomorphic in the population as 0 (`populations.cc`, Stacks
2.68), and divides by `Pi`. Its own columns therefore do not reconcile.
In the example data's `example.sumstats_summary.tsv`, computed the same
way, north's 1 − `Obs_Het`/`Pi` is 0.092 while its `Fis` column reads
0.081; for south, 0.159 against 0.106.

### Heterozygosity per sequenced site

He averaged over variant records is heterozygosity *per variant your
study called*: call more variants and it changes, so it cannot be
compared with other studies. Schmidt et al. (2021) show that the
comparable quantity is heterozygosity per sequenced site. From a SNP VCF
it is one multiplication:

> He<sub>autosomal</sub> = He × (variant records) ÷ (sequenced sites)

`diversity_stats(snps, pops, g, sites = "populations.sumstats_summary.tsv")`
does this for each population separately. It adds up He over the SNPs in
the data (in practice, mean He times the number of SNP records where the
population has at least one genotyped individual) and divides by that
population's own `Sites` from the "All positions (variant and fixed)"
block of the Stacks file. A population's own counts matter: Stacks
counts a site for a population only where it has at least one genotyped
individual (`SumStatsSummary::accumulate()`, Stacks 2.68), and with
several populations and `-p` below their number, a population can be
absent from many records.

Each per-site value gets the same standard errors and bootstrap interval as
Ho or He (`Ho_autosomal_se_combined`, `_lo`, `_hi`, and so on). The
multiplier, (variant records) ÷ (sequenced sites), is a fixed positive number
for each population, so a jackknife SE or a percentile bootstrap bound of the
per-site value is exactly that multiplier times the Ho or He one. This treats
the multiplier as fixed. It leaves out uncertainty in how many SNPs there are
per sequenced site, as the per-site value itself does.

Three conditions apply.

- The records must be single sites, so the conversion is done only for
  the SNP VCF.
- `sites` must describe the loci in the data. Stacks' `Sites` does so
  only for the data exactly as `populations` wrote them. If whole RAD
  loci are removed afterwards (for low call rate or as paralogs), their
  sites should not count, so give `sites` yourself for the loci you
  kept.
- Every SNP of those loci should be in the data. A VCF thinned to one
  SNP per RAD locus leaves most SNPs out, and per-site He comes out far
  too low.

Removing SNPs with a minor allele count or frequency filter lowers
per-site He by the diversity those SNPs carried (section 1). Stacks' own
`Variant_Sites` is deliberately not used as the SNP count: it also
counts SNPs removed after Stacks, and multiplying by it would credit
each removed SNP with the average He of the SNPs kept. After a MAC
filter of 3 with 20 diploids, that would inflate per-site He by 41% under
a neutral site-frequency spectrum: the filter removes 36.5% of the SNPs
but only 10.3% of the diversity (derivation in section 1).
`diversity_stats()` warns when records or whole loci were removed after
reading, or when the VCF's SNP count does not match the Stacks file.

The rescaling cannot account for missing genotypes at monomorphic sites.
An all-sites VCF (`populations --vcf-all`) and `pi_allsites()` handle
missing data site by site instead (Korunes & Samuk 2021), and give
`pi_nc`, the per-site version of Nei & Chesser's He. With little missing
data the two agree closely, as they do in the example data.

### Per polymorphic site: use the pooled denominator

Many RAD-seq papers report He "per polymorphic site". That phrase has
two readings, and they can give opposite answers:

- **pooled**: averaged over sites variable anywhere in the dataset (what
  Stacks' "Variant positions" block and `diversity_stats()` do);
- **within-population**: for each population, averaged only over the
  sites variable in that population.

In a simulation where population B was founded by three individuals from
A (`inst/sims/vignette_sims.R`, part `denominator`), B was less diverse,
but the within-population denominator reversed the difference:

| denominator       | He, population A | He, population B | ratio A:B |
|-------------------|------------------|------------------|-----------|
| pooled            | 0.318            | 0.265            | 1.20      |
| within-population | 0.353            | 0.391            | 0.90      |

The reason: after a bottleneck, B is monomorphic at many sites, and that
is its reduced diversity. Dropping those sites from B's denominator
discards the evidence and keeps only the sites where B retained
variation. So `diversity_stats()` reports the pooled He. The two
versions are linked exactly by He(pooled) = He(within) × `pct_poly`/100,
and `pct_poly` is in the result's `per_population` table, so either can
be recovered if a reader asks.

### Rarefied allelic richness and private alleles

The number of alleles found grows with the number of gene copies
sampled, so populations of different size must be compared at a common
sample size *g* (in gene copies). The expected number of alleles in *g*
copies drawn without replacement from a population's *N* copies is

> A(*g*) = Σ<sub>i</sub> [1 − C(*N* − *N*<sub>i</sub>, *g*)/C(*N*, *g*)]

(Hurlbert 1971; El Mousadik & Petit 1996), where *N*<sub>i</sub> is the
count of allele *i*. The expected number of private alleles at a locus is
the expected number of alleles drawn in one population and in none of
the others, each sampled to *g* copies (Kalinowski 2004; Szpiech et al.
2008). The package reports it added up over the loci where every
population has at least *g* copies (`priv_total`, "rarefied private
alleles" in the summaries), and keeps the per-locus mean as `privAr`.
The count is easier to read ("258 rarefied private alleles"); because
every population is summed over the same loci, the two give the same
comparison between populations. It is an expected value, so it need not
be a whole number. For the same reason, its standard error and interval
are `privAr`'s multiplied by that number of loci.

Both are exact expectations over gene copies, as in HP-RARE and ADZE.
Resampling *individuals* instead would estimate something different when
individuals are inbred, because the two copies inside one individual are
not independent draws.

**Choosing *g*.** A locus counts for a population only where it has at
least *g* gene copies, and for rarefied private alleles only where
*every* population does. A large *g* therefore discards loci with missing data:
compare `Ar_n` and `privAr_n` for two values of *g*
(`vignette("workflow")`, section 5). A good start is *g* = 2 × *r* ×
*n*, rounded down, for Stacks' `-r` value *r* and the smallest
population's *n*. Rarefied private alleles depend on how many other
populations they are compared against, and the count also on how many
loci there are, so neither can be compared between studies.

## 3. Which Stacks file for which statistic

With `--vcf`, Stacks writes one record per SNP (`populations.snps.vcf`)
and one record per RAD locus with haplotype alleles
(`populations.haps.vcf`). With `--write-single-snp` it writes only the
SNP VCF.

| statistic | file | reason |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Ho, He, He per sequenced site | SNP VCF | a per-SNP value means the same in every study |
| FIS | haplotype VCF | a ratio, so the scale cancels; more information per locus |
| rarefied allelic richness | haplotype VCF | at a biallelic SNP it can only be 1 or 2; compare only populations analyzed together |
| rarefied private alleles | haplotype VCF | the same, though it is informative on SNPs too |
| tests between populations | either; say which |  |

### FIS from haplotypes

A RAD locus with three SNPs becomes one marker with up to eight alleles,
and multi-allelic markers carry more information about the heterozygote
deficit. Biallelic SNPs also have a specific weakness: a minor allele
present in a single copy must sit in a heterozygote, which forces Ho =
He and FIS = 0 at that site by arithmetic.

In simulations with a known FIS of 0.10 (`vignette_sims.R`, part
`file_choice`; *n* = 15 and 10, 1,200 RAD loci, 20 replicates), all
three kinds of file were unbiased, and the haplotype file gave the
narrowest interval:

| data                  | FIS   | width of the 95% interval | records |
|-----------------------|-------|---------------------------|---------|
| haplotype VCF         | 0.099 | 0.028                     | 1,200   |
| all SNPs              | 0.099 | 0.031                     | 2,251   |
| one SNP per RAD locus | 0.098 | 0.035                     | 1,200   |

In this simulation, identity by descent is drawn once per individual per
RAD locus, as real inbreeding acts on whole haplotypes. Drawing it
separately for each SNP would make haplotype homozygosity too low and
the haplotype file look worse than it is.

### Ho and He from SNPs

Haplotype gene diversity has a ceiling that rises with the number of
SNPs: a locus with four SNPs can carry many haplotypes, a locus with one
SNP only two (and gene diversity with k haplotypes can be at most 1 −
1/k). Haplotype He therefore depends on read length, enzyme and
SNP-calling settings. In simulations that varied only the number of SNPs
per locus (`vignette_sims.R`, part `snp_density`), haplotype He changed
by 66% across the range and per-SNP He by 24% (part of which is real,
because loci with more SNPs are more variable). Both files gave the same
ratio between two populations (1.14), so either can compare populations
within one study; only the SNP values can be compared with other
studies.

Allelic richness from haplotypes changes about as much, and in one more
way. In the same simulation, haplotype Ar rose by 70% in one population
and 51% in the other as SNPs per locus increased, while per-SNP Ar
(which cannot exceed 2) moved by 6%. Unlike He, the ratio between the
two populations did not stay put: it grew from 1.12 to 1.26. So
haplotype Ar and rarefied private alleles:

- cannot be compared with other studies, unless enzyme, read length, SNP
  calling and filters are all the same;
- can be compared among populations analyzed together (the same Stacks
  run, the same filters and the same *g*), where which population is
  richer is reliable but the size of the difference also depends on SNPs
  per locus;
- are averaged over the loci variable in that run (Stacks writes only
  loci with at least two haplotypes, after `-p` and `-r`), so adding or
  dropping populations from the run changes the loci, as with He per SNP
  (section 2).

**Ho and He are not comparable between the two files.** Haplotype Ho
asks "is this RAD locus heterozygous?", which is true if *any* of its
SNPs is; per-SNP Ho asks it of one site. In the same simulation Ho was
0.42 from haplotypes and 0.32 from SNPs for the same individuals. Label
every table with the file its numbers came from. FIS, a ratio, is
comparable, and FIS from the two files should agree closely; if it does
not, likely causes are sequencing errors creating spurious rare
haplotypes (lowering haplotype FIS), or haplotype genotypes going
missing more often in heterozygotes (Stacks writes a whole haplotype as
missing if any of its SNPs is uncalled; `export_formats.cc`, Stacks
2.68), raising haplotype FIS.

### Linked SNPs and thinning

SNPs on one RAD locus are physically linked and are not independent
replicates. RADdiversity handles this by resampling whole RAD loci for
every standard error and interval (section 4), so linked SNPs move
together. Thinning to one SNP per locus is then unnecessary for these
statistics and discards data, as the table above shows. Analyses that
assume unlinked markers (STRUCTURE, some Ne estimators) do need a
thinned dataset; for those, a random SNP per locus
(`--write-random-snp`, or `filter_thin_one_snp(method = "random")`) is
better than the first, which always sits at the same position relative
to the cut site.

## 4. Uncertainty: how the standard errors are calculated, and which to report

### What a standard error is

A standard error (SE) says how much a number would change if you did the
study again with a new sample. The range from the estimate minus 1.96 SE
to the estimate plus 1.96 SE is a 95% confidence interval: if the study
were repeated many times, about 95 of every 100 such intervals would
contain the true value.

### Two reasons a population's value is uncertain

Imagine you caught 15 fish from a lake and typed 1,000 RAD loci. Your He
could have come out differently for two reasons.

1.  **Which loci.** The 1,000 loci are a sample of the genome. Another
    1,000 would give a slightly different He, because some loci are more
    variable than others.
2.  **Which individuals.** The 15 fish are a sample of the lake. Another
    15 would give a slightly different He. They could give a clearly
    different Ho and FIS if some fish are more inbred than others,
    because an inbred fish is homozygous at many loci at once.

A reported He is a statement about the population's genome, so both
reasons count. Nei & Roychoudhury (1974) split the variance of average
heterozygosity into exactly these two parts.

### How each standard error is calculated

| column | what it resamples | how | holds fixed |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| `_se` | RAD loci | Leave out one RAD locus and recompute; do this for every locus. How much those values spread gives the SE. This is a *jackknife*. | the individuals |
| `_lo`, `_hi` | RAD loci | Draw as many RAD loci as you have, at random and with replacement, and recompute; do this thousands of times. The middle 95% of the results is the interval. This is a *bootstrap*. | the individuals |
| `_se_ind` | individuals | Leave out one individual and recompute; do this for every individual (a jackknife). Computed by default; `se_individuals = FALSE` turns it off. | the loci |
| `_se_combined` | both | Square `_se` and `_se_ind`, add them, and take the square root. Computed by default; `se_individuals = FALSE` turns it off. | nothing |

Three details:

- Whole RAD loci are resampled, not single SNPs. SNPs on one RAD tag are
  inherited together, and resampling them one by one would give
  intervals that are too narrow. hierfstat's `boot.ppfis()` and Stacks'
  `StdErr` columns work SNP by SNP.
- Adding squared SEs is the usual way to combine two separate sources of
  error. Here it errs on the cautious side: the chance of which genotype
  an individual happens to carry at a locus is counted in both SEs, so
  the combined SE is a little too large rather than too small. Owen
  (2007) found the same when resampling both the rows and the columns of
  a data table.
- In the jackknife over individuals, the records each population uses
  are decided once, from all of its individuals, and kept in every
  repeat. Otherwise a record with exactly `min_n` genotyped individuals
  would vanish whenever one of them was left out, the estimate would
  jump, and the SE would come out too large (a jackknife handles such
  jumps badly; Shao & Wu 1989). One case is left: a record with only 2
  genotyped individuals, where leaving one out leaves too few to compute
  He. With 6 individuals per population, when 6% of the records were
  like that the He `_se_ind` was 1.32 times its true value, against 1.10
  with none (part `boundary` of `inst/sims/uncertainty_sources.R`).
  `diversity_stats()` warns above 5%; a higher `min_n` avoids it.

### How we decided which to use for which statistic

We simulated two populations of 15 individuals typed at 1,000 loci,
where the true Ho, He and FIS are known. Each simulated analysis was
repeated 300 times with new loci and new individuals, and we counted how
often each kind of 95% interval contained the true value. A good method
does so about 95% of the time; much less means its intervals are too
narrow. Individuals differed in inbreeding by a standard deviation of F
of 0, 0.10 or 0.25 (`inst/sims/uncertainty_sources.R`, part `main`). The
table gives the range over those three settings.

| statistic | locus SE | locus bootstrap | individual SE | **combined SE** |
|-----------|----------|-----------------|---------------|-----------------|
| Ho        | 41–96%   | 39–95%          | 88–91%        | **93–98%**      |
| He        | 95–96%   | 93–95%          | 72–77%        | **98–99%**      |
| FIS       | 31–94%   | 30–94%          | 92–93%        | **93–98%**      |
| Ar        | 93–94%   | 92–93%          | 98–100%       | 100%            |
| private alleles, per locus | 92–93%   | 91–93%          | 31–36%        | 92–94%          |

What the table shows:

- **Ho and FIS** need the individuals. The locus SE works when
  individuals are alike (96% and 94%) but falls to 41% and 31% when they
  differ a lot in inbreeding.
- **He** needs the loci. It depends mostly on allele frequencies, and an
  inbred individual changes genotypes but hardly frequencies. The
  individual SE alone covered He only 72–77% of the time.
- **The combined SE** covered Ho, He and FIS 93–99% of the time in every
  setting, so no choice has to be made based on g2. It is wider than
  necessary when individuals are alike (1.2 to 1.4 times the true SE)
  and about right when they differ (1.0 to 1.2).
- **Ar and private alleles** are covered by the locus SE alone. Their
  individual SEs were poor: too wide for Ar (1.4 to 1.5 times the true
  SE) and far too small for private alleles, which depend on the other
  populations' individuals too. `diversity_stats()` therefore gives them
  no individual SE. The simulations checked private alleles per locus
  (`privAr`). The reported rarefied private alleles (`priv_total`) are
  that value times the number of loci it is added up over, the same for
  every population, so their SE is `privAr_se` times that number and
  covers the truth as often.

The same pattern held under other conditions (part `robust`): many rare
variants, 8 individuals, 30 individuals at 3,000 loci, 20% missing
genotypes, 4-allele haplotype loci, and individuals that did not differ
in inbreeding.

| statistic | combined SE | locus SE | individual SE |
|-----------|-------------|----------|---------------|
| Ho        | 91–99%      | 45–94%   | 75–93%        |
| He        | 96–98%      | 93–97%   | 47–86%        |
| FIS       | 90–99%      | 30–94%   | 89–94%        |
| Ar        | 97–100%     | 88–96%   | 73–99%        |
| private alleles, per locus | 89–99%      | 89–95%   | 9–91%         |

### The rule

> **Ho, He and FIS:** report `_se_combined`, which `diversity_stats()`
> computes by default (`se_individuals = TRUE`). A 95% interval is the
> estimate ± 1.96 × `_se_combined`. The per-site Ho and He take the same
> rule: report `Ho_autosomal_se_combined` and `He_autosomal_se_combined`.
>
> **Ar and rarefied private alleles:** report `_se`. The bootstrap interval `_lo` to
> `_hi` is also available; in these simulations it held the true value about
> as often as the SE, or slightly less often (Ar: 92–93% against 93–94%).

The short `summary()` of `diversity_stats()` shows only these recommended
standard errors, and says which kind each one is. It quotes the wider ranges
over all the simulated settings (the second table above): 90–99% for the
combined SE of Ho, He and FIS, and 88–96% for the locus SE of Ar and rarefied
private alleles.
For He alone the locus SE was also close (95–96%); the combined SE is used for
all three so that the choice does not depend on how much individuals differ
in inbreeding.

No simulation has checked the standard errors of FST, D, beta, pi, `dxy` and
`da_nc` (`differentiation_stats()`, `pi_allsites()`). They are jackknifes over RAD
loci only, and their summaries say "not checked by simulation". The
heterozygosity test of `het_between_pops()` is different: its combined test
has its own simulation, with a false-positive rate of 3–7.5% when populations
do not differ, against up to 30% for Welch's t alone
(`inst/sims/het_test_null.R`).

### Why not bootstrap individuals?

A bootstrap over individuals draws 15 individuals at random *with
replacement*, so a typical draw contains only about 10 different
individuals, some of them twice. He's small-sample correction and
rarefaction both assume every individual in the sample is a different
one. A repeated individual makes the sample look less diverse than it
is, so the bootstrap values sit too low, and because the number of
different individuals changes from draw to draw they also spread too
widely. In the simulation above, intervals from `boot = "individuals"`
contained the true He 6–8% of the time and the true Ar 0% of the time;
resampling individuals and loci together (`boot = "both"`, Owen & Eckles
2012) did little better (He 28–33%, Ar 1–3%). Both modes are kept only
for comparison with software that uses them.

For reference, diveRsity's `divBasic()` resamples individuals and
computes He as the uncorrected 1 − Σ*p*<sup>2</sup> (GitHub source,
`R/divBasic.R`), so its intervals describe a different, plug-in
estimator.

### What no standard error covers

- **Relatives.** When the sample was 5 families of 3 full siblings, He
  and FIS were themselves too low, by almost 4 true SEs, and even the
  combined SE covered them only 9% and 16% of the time. Siblings carry
  copies of the same parental genes, so they look less diverse than the
  population. Screen for relatives with `kinship_check()` (section 7).
- **Filtering and allele dropout.** These shift the estimate itself
  (sections 1 and 5).
- **Linkage between separate RAD loci.** Loci close together on a
  chromosome are not independent; `locus_from = "window"` in
  `read_stacks_vcf()` groups nearby records into one resampling unit.

### Stacks' StdErr columns

Stacks' `populations.sumstats_summary.tsv` reports `StdErr` as the
standard deviation over variant sites divided by √(number of sites)
(`SumStatsSummary::final_calculation()`, Stacks 2.68). That treats every
SNP as independent, so it is narrower than an interval over RAD loci. In
Stacks 2.68 the `StdErr` printed for `Fis` is computed from `Num_Indv`'s
variance (`populations.cc`, line 3108), which is a bug in Stacks 2.68;
check it against your own Stacks version before relying on that column.

## 5. Comparing populations

### Two ways to get the test wrong

Section 4 showed that a population's value is uncertain for two reasons:
which loci were typed, and which individuals were caught. A test between
populations must count both. Common tests count only one.

- **Loci only.** A bootstrap over loci, or a paired test on per-locus
  values, treats loci as the replicates. But every locus is measured on
  the same few individuals. When individuals differ in inbreeding, an
  inbred individual is homozygous at many loci at once, and adding loci
  does not average that away. The interval becomes far too narrow. Van
  Dongen (1995) made this point for allozyme data.
- **Individuals only.** Welch's *t* on one heterozygosity value per
  individual treats the loci as fixed. But even two populations with the
  same genome-wide heterozygosity differ a little at any given set of
  loci, because drift changes allele frequencies at each locus
  separately. The more differentiated the populations, the bigger that
  chance difference.

`het_between_pops_selftest()` simulates two populations with *identical*
true heterozygosity, each with its own allele frequencies (n = 15 and
10, 1,500 loci), so every significant result is a false positive. At a
nominal 5%:

| setting | combined test | Welch's *t* | locus bootstrap |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| not differentiated, individuals differ in inbreeding (SD of F 0.10) | 5% | 6% | 53% |
| differentiated (FST 0.10), individuals alike | 6% | 14% | 7% |
| differentiated, individuals differ | 5% | 6% | 39% |

A larger grid (`inst/sims/het_test_null.R`: FST 0 to 0.2, SD of F 0 to
0.1, 15 + 10 or 30 + 30 individuals, 1,000 or 10,000 loci, 400 repeats
each) gave the same picture. Welch's *t* alone rejected up to 14% of the
time at FST 0.05 and up to 30% at FST 0.2 when individuals were alike,
and more often with more individuals; adding loci did not help. The
combined test stayed between 3% and 7.5% in every setting.

### The test `het_between_pops()` uses

***NOTE: each part of this test is standard (Welch's variance over
individuals, a jackknife over RAD loci). As far as I know, no
population-genetics software combines them to compare populations, so
the combination is new and not yet peer reviewed. Keep this in mind when
using it. –N. Whelan (September 8, 2026).***

`het_between_pops()` gives each individual one number, its
heterozygosity over the loci both populations of a pair clear `min_call`
at. The difference between the two population means has a standard
error, `se_combined`, with two parts:

1.  how much individuals vary, the same variance Welch's *t* uses;
2.  how much the difference would change if other loci had been typed: a
    jackknife over RAD loci (leave out one RAD locus at a time).

Part 2 also contains some chance from which genotypes the sampled
individuals carry at each locus, and part 1 already counts that. So it
is estimated and taken out of part 2 before the two are added (the same
double counting noted for `_se_combined` in section 4; Owen 2007). The
confidence interval (`ci_lo`, `ci_hi`) and `p_combined` use a *t*
distribution with Welch-Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. When
individuals differ a lot in inbreeding, part 1 dominates and the result
is close to Welch's *t*; when populations are differentiated and
individuals are alike, part 2 matters.

The table also gives `p_welch` and the Wilcoxon rank-sum `p_wilcox`
(individuals only) for comparison, and Hedges' *g*, the difference in
units of the among-individual standard deviation.

Two questions use the same machinery. Mean individual heterozygosity is
the population's **observed** heterozygosity, He × (1 − F). It asks
whether populations differ in heterozygosity, which reflects both how
diverse and how inbred they are: two populations with the same He differ
here if one is more inbred. (To compare He itself, use
`diversity_stats()`.) The individual inbreeding coefficient F = 1 −
(observed heterozygous loci)/(expected), with the expectation from the
individual's own population, asks whether they differ in **inbreeding**;
its population mean equals FIS when every individual is typed at every
locus (`?individual_inbreeding`).

With three or more populations, report the overall test first
(`omnibus`: Welch's one-way ANOVA and Kruskal-Wallis), then the pairwise
tests with Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-values. The overall tests use
individuals only, so with differentiated populations whose individuals
are alike in inbreeding they reject too readily; confirm a difference
with the pairs' `p_combined_BH`.

### Checks before reporting

- **Relatives.** Relatives are not independent individuals, and one
  family can dominate a small sample; screen with `kinship_check()`
  (section 7).
- **Missing data.** If poorly sequenced individuals are both more often
  missing and, through allele dropout, more often called homozygous, a
  difference between populations can be a difference in library quality.
  `het_between_pops()` correlates each individual's call rate with its
  heterozygosity and flags a positive correlation.
- **g2.** Whether individuals differ in inbreeding (David et al. 2007).
  When they do, heterozygosity is correlated across loci within an
  individual, and that is exactly when a locus-based test goes wrong.
  g2 assumes the two loci of each pair are inherited independently, and
  SNPs on one RAD locus are not: an individual with two different
  haplotypes is heterozygous at several of them at once. So pairs of
  SNPs on the same RAD locus are left out, and the permutation test
  moves a RAD locus's SNPs together. Before this was done, in
  simulations with 20 individuals, no inbreeding and about two SNPs per
  RAD locus, the test found g2 above 0 in 54–56% of runs, at 500 to 8,000
  loci; after, in 2–4% (nominal 5%). Real variance in inbreeding was still
  found every time (`inst/sims/g2_linked_snps.R`). SNP and haplotype VCFs
  now both work. With few individuals, test g2 > 0 with the permutation
  p-value, not the bootstrap interval. With no inbreeding, the 95%
  interval missed 0 in 17–19% of simulated data sets with 8 individuals,
  10–15% with 15 and 7% with 30, nearly always by lying below 0; the
  permutation test rejected in 2–5% (`inst/sims/g2_ci_small_n.R`).
- **Sex-linked loci.** In the sex with one copy of a sex chromosome (XY
  males, ZW females), loci on it look homozygous. They raise FIS and
  lower those individuals' heterozygosity. If the samples differ in sex
  ratio, a difference in heterozygosity can come from that. De novo RAD
  loci cannot be sorted by chromosome; loci heterozygous in only one
  sex, or genotyped in only one sex, are the usual clue.
- **Power.** Power is set by the number of individuals, not loci. With
  15 and 10 individuals and an among-individual SD of F of 0.10, Welch's
  test detected a difference in mean F of 0.05 (0.5 SD) 17% of the time
  and of 0.08 (0.8 SD) 39% of the time (`vignette_sims.R`, part
  `power`). A non-significant result from such samples is weak evidence
  of no difference.

### Null alleles and allele dropout

A mutation in a restriction site stops a chromosome from producing
reads, so its carrier looks homozygous for its other allele, or is
missing if both copies drop out. This "allele dropout" inflates FIS. It
is also more common at more variable loci and in more diverse
populations (Gautier et al. 2013; Arnold et al. 2013), so it does not
affect every population equally: it can understate a real difference in
He, and it can create a difference in FIS.

Depth filters do not remove it. `diversity_stats()` returns
`fis_by_call_rate`, which groups each population's loci by its own call
rate there: dropout makes FIS rise as call rate falls, while inbreeding
raises FIS at every locus alike. If FIS rises, report FIS from
well-typed loci (`complete_case = TRUE` or a higher `min_n`) as well.

How well does this check work? In simulations with a true FIS of 0.10
(15 + 15 individuals, 2,000 loci, 100 repeats each; `vignette_sims.R`,
part `dropout`), "FIS in the lowest call-rate group is more than 1.96
standard errors above the highest" gave these results:

| what was simulated | flagged | FIS, all loci | FIS, loci typed in everyone |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| missing genotypes at random | 2% | 0.100 | 0.101 |
| missing genotypes clustered by locus, at random | 4% | 0.099 | 0.099 |
| poorly covered loci (25% missing, 30% of heterozygotes called homozygous) | 100% | 0.181 | 0.102 |
| null allele at 25% of loci, frequency 0.2 | 100% | 0.173 | 0.135 |
| null allele at 10% of loci, frequency 0.1 | 23% | 0.116 | 0.112 |

So false alarms are rare, and strong dropout is found. Weak dropout is
often missed, but it also changes FIS little. Restricting to fully typed
loci removes dropout from poor coverage, but only part of a null
allele's effect: one null copy hides a heterozygote without making the
genotype missing.

## 6. Differentiation

### FST

`differentiation_stats()` computes Weir & Cockerham's (1984) FST from
its variance components *a*, *b* and *c*, summed over loci before taking
the ratio (FST = Σ*a*/Σ(*a* + *b* + *c*)), for all populations and for
each pair. The implementation matches `hierfstat::wc()` to machine
precision on records typed in at least two of the compared populations
(package tests).

One choice differs from hierfstat. A record where only one of the
compared populations has any genotyped individual says nothing about
differences between them, yet its within-population variance would enter
the denominator and pull FST toward 0. Such records are common with
three or more populations and `-p` below their number. RADdiversity
skips them, as VCFtools and Stacks' own pairwise FST do;
`hierfstat::wc()` keeps them. The number skipped is in
`settings$fst_records_skipped`.

### Jost's D and beta

FST cannot reach 1 when loci are highly variable, even for populations
that share no alleles, so FST from many-haplotype RAD loci is not
comparable with FST from SNPs. Jost's (2008) D is built to avoid that
ceiling. D is computed from Hs and Ht averaged over loci (not by
averaging per-locus D), following the steps of the mmod package (Winter
2012; see `inst/NOTICE`). Hs and Ht are Nei & Chesser's estimators,
which use H<sub>o</sub>, for the reason given in section 2; this is also
how `hierfstat::basic.stats()` computes `Dest`. mmod's version corrects
Hs by 2*N*/(2*N* − 1), which assumes random mating: with inbred
individuals its D comes out too high. In a test with two samples from
the same population (true D = 0), 8 individuals each and *F* = 0.4, it
gave D = 0.017, 29 standard errors above 0; the Nei & Chesser version
gave a value within 3 standard errors of 0. On the example data, where
*F* ≈ 0.1, the difference is about 7% of D. Weir & Goudet's (2017) beta,
via hierfstat, is a third measure; it is a point estimate only, and slow
on large datasets (`beta = FALSE` skips it).

**The global D uses only records genotyped in every population.** Jost's
D for *k* populations measures differentiation among those *k*
populations. A record where some of them are untyped measures it among a
different, smaller set, and averaging such records in biases the global
D: for three completely differentiated populations (true D = 1), one of
them untyped at half the records, it came out at 0.875 (package tests).
So the global D skips those records, and `D_records` in the result,
`print()` and `summary()` report how many records it rests on. Each
pairwise D uses every record typed in both of its populations, and FST
uses every record typed in at least two populations, because Weir &
Cockerham's estimator handles a varying number of populations per
record.

Report D (or beta) alongside FST for haplotype data. Intervals for FST
and D come from the same bootstrap over RAD loci as everything else.

### Isolation by distance

When individuals mostly mate near where they were born, populations far
apart share fewer genes than neighbors. Differentiation then grows with
distance: isolation by distance (Wright 1943). `isolation_by_distance()`
tests for this with the pairwise FST or D from `differentiation_stats()`
and a table of distances (`read_distances()`).

**What is compared.** Rousset (1997) showed that FST/(1 − FST) for a
pair of populations rises in a straight line:

- with the distance itself in a **1-D habitat** (a river, a coastline);
- with the natural log of the distance in a **2-D habitat** (an area).

The slope measures dispersal. 1/slope estimates 4 × density × σ² in 1-D
and 4π × density × σ² in 2-D. Here density is individuals per unit of
length or area, and σ² is the mean squared distance between parent and
offspring along one axis. This holds best for pairs farther apart than
σ, in populations near equilibrium. Which habitat is right depends on
the organism, so `habitat` has no default: you must choose `"1D"` or
`"2D"`.

**Why D is used as it is, not as D/(1 − D).** Write Q₀ for the chance
that two genes from the same population are identical, and Q<sub>d</sub>
for two genes from populations at distance *d*. For a pair of
populations:

| statistic | in these terms |
|---|---|
| FST/(1 − FST) | (Q₀ − Q<sub>d</sub>) / (1 − Q₀) |
| D | (Q₀ − Q<sub>d</sub>) / Q₀ |
| D/(1 − D) | (Q₀ − Q<sub>d</sub>) / Q<sub>d</sub> |

Rousset's straight line comes from the top part, Q₀ − Q<sub>d</sub>.
FST/(1 − FST) and D divide it by numbers that do not change with
distance, when the populations are about equally diverse. So
D = FST/(1 − FST) × H<sub>s</sub>/(1 − H<sub>s</sub>): D is a straight
line whenever FST/(1 − FST) is. D/(1 − D) divides by Q<sub>d</sub>,
which falls with distance, so its line bends upward, and more so the
larger D is.

We checked this with exact identity probabilities in stepping-stone
models, at distances of 2 to 20 steps (`inst/sims/ibd_d_transform.R`;
no sampling noise). "Bend" is the slope over the far half of the
distances divided by the slope over the near half; 1 is a straight
line.

| setting | D | bend of FST/(1 − FST) | bend of D | bend of D/(1 − D) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1-D, low mutation | 0.002–0.06 | 0.97–0.99 | the same | 1.01–1.03 |
| 1-D, higher mutation | 0.02–0.47 | 0.74–0.91 | the same | 1.10–1.35 |
| 2-D | 0.19–0.90 | 0.78–0.99 | the same | 1.41–4.44 |

In every setting, D ÷ [FST/(1 − FST)] equaled
H<sub>s</sub>/(1 − H<sub>s</sub>). Where FST/(1 − FST) itself bends
(higher mutation, as distances approach the limit of Rousset's
approximation), D/(1 − D) bends the other way by an amount set by the
size of D, not by dispersal, so it does not correct that.

A Mantel test on D/(1 − D) would still keep its false-positive rate (any
permutation test does), and with ranks (`method = "spearman"`) it gives
the same answer as D. But nothing supports it, so it is not offered.
The slope of D equals the FST slope times H<sub>s</sub>/(1 − H<sub>s</sub>),
so it depends on diversity as well as dispersal. The package reports it,
but only the FST slope estimates dispersal.

**The Mantel test.** The pairs share populations (a–b and a–c both
contain a), so the correlation *r* between genetic and geographic values
cannot be tested like an ordinary correlation. The Mantel test (Mantel
1967) shuffles the populations among the places and recomputes *r* each
time. The p-value is the share of orderings that give an *r* at least
as large as the data's. It is one-sided, because isolation by distance
predicts a positive *r*. With 7 or fewer populations every ordering is
tried, so the p-value is exact and the same on every run. With more,
9,999 random orderings are used, and p = (b + 1)/(9,999 + 1), where b
counts those at least as large (Phipson & Smyth 2010). With few
populations the test has little power:

| populations | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 or more |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| orderings | 6 | 24 | 120 | 720 | 5,040 | 9,999 random |
| smallest possible p | 0.17 | 0.042 | 0.0083 | 0.0014 | 0.0002 | 0.0001 |

The smallest p is larger when the distances are symmetric. For example,
evenly spaced sites give the same *r* in reverse order, so 4 evenly
spaced sites cannot go below 2/24 = 0.083. With 7 or fewer populations,
the summary's checks give the smallest p for your own distances.

Guillot & Rousset (2013) showed that this simple Mantel test is valid
for isolation by distance: with no isolation by distance, the genetic
data could be shuffled among the places without changing their
distribution, which is what the test assumes. They also showed that
**partial** Mantel tests (for example, distance plus a barrier or a
habitat matrix) are not valid for spatially structured data, so the
package does not offer them. The package tests check that *r* and the
exact p-value match `vegan::mantel()` (Oksanen et al.).

**The slope has no interval here.** The slope is a least-squares line
through all pairs. The pairs are not independent, so the usual
regression standard error would be wrong, and none is given. Genepop
(Rousset 2008) gives a bootstrap interval over loci for the slope; use
it if you need one.

**Negative values.** A pairwise FST or D can be estimated slightly below
0 when two populations barely differ. Such values are kept: setting them
to 0 would bias the slope.

## 7. Relatives and Hardy-Weinberg tests

### Screening for relatives

`kinship_check()` estimates kinship for every pair with KING-robust
(Manichaikul et al. 2010), which uses no allele frequencies and so is
not misled by population structure, or with Goudet's beta (Goudet, Kay &
Weir 2018) via hierfstat. A benchmark on reduced-representation data
from non-model species (McMaster et al. 2025) found KING precise but
insensitive (it misses many true relatives) and beta sensitive but
imprecise, worse under structure and inbreeding. Treat both as screens:
a flagged pair deserves a look, and an empty list is not proof there are
no relatives. KING also assumes individuals are not inbred. Two
unrelated individuals with inbreeding coefficient *F* read about −*F*/(1
− *F*) (−0.11 at *F* = 0.1), and relatives read lower too, so they can
fall below the cutpoints. A heterozygote deficit from pooling
subpopulations (a Wahlund effect) does not do this, because relatives
share a subpopulation.

Two details. The package uses Manichaikul et al.'s estimator with the
**sum** of the two individuals' heterozygote counts in the denominator.
PLINK 2's `--make-king` uses their between-family version, built on the
smaller count, which reads lower when one individual's heterozygotes
were under-called. With 20% of one individual's heterozygotes called
homozygous, a parent-offspring pair (true 0.25) reads 0.167 with the sum
and 0.125 with PLINK 2's version. And beta compares each pair with the
average pair it is given, so on several differentiated populations
pooled, unrelated members of the same population look related (80% of
them in a simulation at F<sub>ST</sub> = 0.1); with `popmap`, beta is
computed within each population, and none were.

### Hardy-Weinberg tests

`hwe_test()` runs the exact test of Hardy-Weinberg proportions (Levene
1949; Haldane 1954): exactly, by listing every possible table, for
biallelic loci (the test PLINK and VCFtools use; Wigginton et al. 2005),
and by Guo & Thompson's (1992) direct Monte Carlo method for
multi-allelic haplotype loci, stopping early once a p-value is clearly
not small (Besag & Clifford 1991). Each locus gets `F`, the direction of
any departure. It is a report, never a filter (section 1). Loci with a
heterozygote excess in every population are candidate paralogs worth
inspecting.

## Appendix A. Stacks columns and RADdiversity

Notation: *N* diploid individuals genotyped at a site, 2*N* gene copies,
allele frequencies *p*<sub>i</sub>, observed heterozygosity
*H*<sub>o</sub>.

| quantity | formula | Stacks column | RADdiversity |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| observed heterozygosity | heterozygotes / *N* | `Obs_Het` | `Ho` |
| gene diversity, plug-in | 1 − Σ*p*<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup> | `Exp_Het` | not reported |
| gene diversity, 2*N*-corrected | (2*N*/(2*N* − 1))(1 − Σ*p*<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup>) | `Pi` | `He_2n_corr` |
| gene diversity, Nei & Chesser | (*N*/(*N* − 1))(1 − Σ*p*<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup> − *H*<sub>o</sub>/(2*N*)) | not available | `He` |
| FIS at a site | 1 − *H*<sub>o</sub>/(gene diversity) | `Fis`, using `Pi` | not reported per site |
| FIS over sites | mean of per-site FIS (Stacks); 1 − Σ*H*<sub>o</sub>/Σ*H*<sub>s</sub> (RADdiversity) | `Fis` | `Fis` |
| per-site diversity | mean over all sequenced sites | `Pi`, All-positions block | `He_autosomal`, `pi_nc` |
| private alleles | raw count | `Private` | `priv_total` (rarefied count; `privAr` per locus) |

Stacks computes `Pi` at a site as the chance that two of the gene copies
typed there differ, counted pair by pair: `Pi` = 1 − Σ
C(*n*<sub>i</sub>, 2) / C(*n*, 2) for *n* gene copies carrying allele
counts *n*<sub>i</sub> (Hohenlohe et al. 2010), which is the same number
as (*n*/(*n* − 1))(1 − Σ*p*<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup>) in the table above.
Stacks' `Pi` therefore estimates the same parameter as `He` and differs
from it by about *F*/(2*N* − 1); `diversity_stats()` prints both. Its
`Fis` differs from RADdiversity's in both the denominator (`Pi`) and the
averaging (section 2). The per-site `Pi` in the "Variant positions"
block is per variant site, not nucleotide diversity; only the "All
positions (variant and fixed)" block is per sequenced site.

To check your own Stacks version, take a row of
`populations.sumstats.tsv` and confirm `Pi` = `Exp_Het` × 2*N*/(2*N* −
1) and `Fis` = (`Pi` − `Obs_Het`)/`Pi`. `diversity_core_selftest()`
checks these against rows of published Stacks output.

## Appendix B. How other tools compare

Checked against the named versions; later versions may differ.

|   | RADdiversity | hierfstat 0.5.11 | diveRsity (GitHub source) | Stacks 2.68 |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| He estimator | Nei & Chesser | Nei & Chesser (`basic.stats`) | plug-in 1 − Σ*p*<sup>2</sup> | 2*N*-corrected `Pi` |
| FIS over loci | ratio of sums | ratio of sums (`basic.stats` overall) | not checked | mean of per-site ratios |
| resampling unit | RAD loci, and individuals for `_se_ind` / `_se_combined` | loci as rows (`boot.ppfis`, `boot.ppfst`, `boot.vc`) | individuals (`divBasic`) | none; SD/√sites |
| rarefied private alleles | yes, with SE | no | no | no |
| FST at records typed in one population | skipped | kept (`wc`) | — | skipped |
| global D at records missing a population | skipped | — | — | — |
| Hs inside Jost's D | Nei & Chesser | Nei & Chesser (`basic.stats` `Dest`) | not checked | not checked |

## Appendix C. Where the numbers come from

| claim | source |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| bias of the 2*N*-corrected He and of FIS built on it; FIS reaches −1 | `diversity_core_selftest()` |
| FIS unbiased under locus-driven missing data | `diversity_core_selftest()` |
| share of π, and of SNPs, at sites with minor allele count ≤ 2 | derivation in section 1 |
| per-site He 41% too high if scaled by `Variant_Sites` after a MAC filter | the same derivation (section 1) |
| records surviving `complete_case` | (1 − *m*)<sup>25</sup> |
| pooled vs within-population denominator | `inst/sims/vignette_sims.R`, part `denominator` |
| FIS precision by file | `inst/sims/vignette_sims.R`, part `file_choice` |
| haplotype vs SNP He and Ar as SNP density varies | `inst/sims/vignette_sims.R`, part `snp_density` |
| coverage of locus, individual and combined SEs, and of the bootstraps | `inst/sims/uncertainty_sources.R`, parts `main` and `robust` |
| individual SEs with records of 2 genotyped individuals | `inst/sims/uncertainty_sources.R`, part `boundary` |
| false-positive rates of the combined test, Welch's *t* and a locus bootstrap | `het_between_pops_selftest()`; the full grid in `inst/sims/het_test_null.R` |
| power of Welch's test | `inst/sims/vignette_sims.R`, part `power` |
| how well `fis_by_call_rate` detects dropout | `inst/sims/vignette_sims.R`, part `dropout` |
| Jost's D with inbred individuals; match with hierfstat's `Dest` | package tests (`test-differentiation-stats.R`) |
| g2 with several SNPs per RAD locus, before and after leaving out same-locus pairs | `inst/sims/g2_linked_snps.R` |
| g2's bootstrap interval and permutation test with 8, 15 and 30 individuals | `inst/sims/g2_ci_small_n.R` |
| KING's two estimators under allele dropout; beta on pooled populations | `inst/sims/kinship_checks.R` |
| D vs D/(1 − D) under isolation by distance | `inst/sims/ibd_d_transform.R` |
| Mantel *r* and exact p-value match `vegan::mantel()` | package tests (`test-isolation-by-distance.R`) |
| Stacks formulas and averaging | Stacks 2.68 source files named in the text; rows of published Stacks output in `diversity_core_selftest()` |
